explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The lament says Pharaoh is like a monster in the seas, and then it says, "You thrash about in your rivers…" (Ezekiel 32:2). Those rivers are his own backyard. A monster making a big scene in his own backyard is still a monster making a big scene.

I get the guess, since Egypt does make you think of sand. But the lament puts this monster in water. It says, "You thrash about in your rivers…" (Ezekiel 32:2). A sea monster in the desert would just be a very lost monster.

Hills are a stretch, friend. This monster is a thing of the seas, and the lament says he thrashes about "…in your rivers…" (Ezekiel 32:2). Mountains show up later in the passage, but they're not where he splashes. Stay near the water on this one.

Not quite, baker. The lament says the opposite. Pharaoh is "…churning up the waters with your feet and muddying the streams." (Ezekiel 32:2). Clear streams don't come from a monster stomping around in them. That's like trying to keep a counter clean while I dive face-first into the chocolate chips.

Right, baker. Pharaoh doesn't keep anything clear. The lament says he is "…churning up the waters with your feet and muddying the streams." (Ezekiel 32:2). I've made a mess on my own counter before, so I won't judge.

That's it, baker. The Lord GOD says, "I will spread My net over you…" (Ezekiel 32:3). Pharaoh was thrashing around like he owned the water. Now God has a net out, and nobody thrashes his way out of that.

A cloak sounds cozy, friend, but this isn't a cozy moment. The Lord GOD says, "I will spread My net over you…" (Ezekiel 32:3). A net is for catching a monster, and a cloak is for a chilly evening. Big difference.

Close on the spreading part, but this isn't a tent. The Lord GOD says, "I will spread My net over you…" (Ezekiel 32:3). Fishing for a sea monster calls for a net. Nobody ever caught a monster by putting up a tent and hoping.

Yes, baker. God says, "I will abandon you on the land and hurl you into the open field." (Ezekiel 32:4). The net draws him up out of the water, and he ends up on the land. An open field is where he gets left. That's a long way from the rivers he was thrashing around in.

Going back to the water is a natural guess, friend. But God says the opposite: "I will abandon you on the land and hurl you into the open field." (Ezekiel 32:4). The net draws him up, and the land and the open field are where he's left.
A well is a creative guess, friend. But the text says, "I will abandon you on the land and hurl you into the open field." (Ezekiel 32:4). The place named is an open field.

True, baker. God says, "I will cause all the birds of the air to settle upon you…" (Ezekiel 32:4). The birds are in the picture along with the beasts. It's a heavy part of the lament, and I think it's meant to show how far Pharaoh has fallen.

It's actually true, friend. God says, "I will cause all the birds of the air to settle upon you…" (Ezekiel 32:4). The birds are right there in the verse. It's a heavy picture, and the text doesn't soften it.

Not this time, baker. It's way bigger than one small spot. God says, "I will put your flesh on the mountains and fill the valleys with your remains." (Ezekiel 32:5). Mountains and valleys are a lot of ground.

Right, baker. It isn't one small spot at all. God says, "I will put your flesh on the mountains and fill the valleys with your remains." (Ezekiel 32:5). Mountains and valleys cover a whole lot of ground.

That's right, baker. God says, "I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light." (Ezekiel 32:7). He also says He will "…darken their stars." and bring darkness on Egypt's land (Ezekiel 32:7-8). Even the sky goes quiet over this fall. When the lights go out up there, you know it's serious.

I see the thinking, but it goes the other way. God says He will "…darken their stars." and that the moon "…will not give its light." (Ezekiel 32:7). The shining lights in the heavens get dimmed over Pharaoh (Ezekiel 32:8). This isn't a bright moment, friend.

Falling is a dramatic guess, friend, but it isn't what the text says. The sun gets covered with a cloud, the moon "…will not give its light." and the stars are darkened (Ezekiel 32:7). Darkened is the word, not fallen.

You got it, baker. God says, "…their kings will shudder in horror because of you when I brandish My sword before them." (Ezekiel 32:10). Pharaoh's fall shakes up many peoples and their kings. When something that big drops, a lot of folks feel it.
Rescue isn't what the verse says, friend. God says the kings "…will shudder in horror because of you when I brandish My sword before them." (Ezekiel 32:10). Their reaction is horror.

That's a clever guess, but the verse is about fear. God says the kings "…will shudder in horror because of you…" (Ezekiel 32:10). Taking over land doesn't come up here. These kings are shaking, not shopping for property.

explanations.answer: The most ruthless of all nations
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, "I will make your hordes fall by the swords of the mighty, the most ruthless of all nations." (Ezekiel 32:12). That's how the text itself describes them. They're described by how hard they are, not how old or rich.

Age isn't what God points to here, friend. He says the mighty ones are "…the most ruthless of all nations." (Ezekiel 32:12). The verse doesn't say a thing about how old they are. I've been in a drawer long enough to know age isn't the point anyway.

Money isn't in the verse, baker. God calls the mighty ones "…the most ruthless of all nations." (Ezekiel 32:12). The text is describing how they fight, not what they have in the bank. That's a different kind of bake entirely.
True, baker. God says, "They will ravage the pride of Egypt and all her multitudes will be destroyed." (Ezekiel 32:12). Pride and multitudes both go down in that verse. It's a big, sobering line.

It's actually true, friend. God says, "They will ravage the pride of Egypt and all her multitudes will be destroyed." (Ezekiel 32:12). The verse says all her multitudes, not just some of them. It's a heavy line and the text doesn't water it down.

Other way around, baker. God says, "No human foot will muddy them again, and no cattle hooves will disturb them." (Ezekiel 32:13). Remember the monster muddying the streams in verse 2? That stops. The waters finally get left alone.

Right, baker. God says, "No human foot will muddy them again, and no cattle hooves will disturb them." (Ezekiel 32:13). The stirring is over, and that's a real change from the thrashing in verse 2. It's like a kitchen that finally goes quiet after the whole family leaves.
That's the word, baker. God says, "Then I will let her waters settle and will make her rivers flow like oil…" (Ezekiel 32:14). The waters settle, and the rivers flow like oil.
Rising isn't the word, friend. God says, "Then I will let her waters settle and will make her rivers flow like oil…" (Ezekiel 32:14). Settle is the word the verse uses.
Boiling isn't the word, baker. God says, "Then I will let her waters settle…" (Ezekiel 32:14). He also says He will make her rivers flow like oil.
That's right, baker. God says, "…then they will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 32:15). What comes to be known is who He is.
Not in this verse, friend. God says Egypt becomes a desolation and then "…they will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 32:15). What comes to be known there is who He is.

That's not what the verse says, baker. God says He will empty Egypt "…of all that filled it…" and then "…they will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 32:15). What comes to be known is who He is. Nothing is said here about Egypt rising again.

True, baker. God says, "This is the lament they will chant for her; the daughters of the nations will chant it." (Ezekiel 32:16). The daughters of the nations are the ones who chant it. A lament that big needs a big choir.

It's actually true, friend. God says, "This is the lament they will chant for her; the daughters of the nations will chant it." (Ezekiel 32:16). The daughters of the nations are named right there. They chant it over Egypt and all her multitudes.
